## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. Skill guides still apply for domain knowledge (query syntax, attribute and metric names, pitfalls), but where a guide tells you to call a specific read tool such as `search_datadog_logs`, `analyze_datadog_logs`, or `get_datadog_metric`, make the equivalent call from `execute_code` instead, using `search_datadog_sdk` to find it. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. Use the named tool only when `search_datadog_sdk` finds no operation for what you need, or when `execute_code` still fails for a step after following its own error guidance. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. <system-reminder>
# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. Skill guides still apply for domain knowledge (query syntax, attribute and metric names, pitfalls), but where a guide tells you to call a specific read tool such as `search_datadog_logs`, `analyze_datadog_logs`, or `get_datadog_metric`, make the equivalent call from `execute_code` instead, using `search_datadog_sdk` to find it. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. Use the named tool only when `search_datadog_sdk` finds no operation for what you need, or when `execute_code` still fails for a step after following its own error guidance. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. Skill guides still apply for domain knowledge (query syntax, attribute and metric names, pitfalls), but where a guide tells you to call a specific read tool such as `search_datadog_logs`, `analyze_datadog_logs`, or `get_datadog_metric`, make the equivalent call from `execute_code` instead, using `search_datadog_sdk` to find it. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. Use the named tool only when `search_datadog_sdk` finds no operation for what you need, or when `execute_code` still fails for a step after following its own error guidance. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

{"additions":827,"author":{"id":"MDQ6VXNlcjI2OTQwNTEx","is_bot":false,"login":"Beehtrix","name":""},"baseRefName":"main","body":"Related to #412 and #534. Not marked as fixing them: #557 already fixed the main symptom (compact transcripts reading as empty), and I don't know whether you consider those issues done.

This is rebased onto `main` 6c4b11de and merges cleanly with current `main` (fb99b029). That brings in #575's split scan-cache versions, #589's privacy-layer removal and #590's flat fact store. I adjusted the versioning to fit, as described below. If you'd rather not take it, or want it split, say so and I'll adjust or close it.

The commits don't carry `Entire-Checkpoint` trailers: I don't have a supported agent session to capture them from, and I didn't want to fake any.

## What #557 already does

It reads top-level `content` for compact records in the conversation, history-fragment and eval-gen readers. Two of my new tests (`TestScanConversationCompactTranscript`, `TestHistoryIndexesDefaultCompactExport`) pass on unmodified main.

## What this PR still adds

Three of my new tests still fail on main 6c4b11de (re-run after the rebase): `TestExtractHistoryJSONFragmentsCompactTranscript`, `TestHistoryIndexBuildsRecordsFromCompactTranscript` and `TestHistoryDeltaRescansOverlayFromPreCompactReader`.

- **Tool output in code facts.** Compact transcripts inline tool output as `tool_use.result.output`, with no separate `tool_result` record. `extractContentFragments` now mines it, so compact sessions get code facts. Native transcripts have no `result` key, so nothing changes for them.
- **Rebuild stale history indexes.** The history source manifest stores `extraction_version`, and `historyIndexCurrent` treats an index built with another version as stale. Without it, a plain `refresh` with unchanged transcripts keeps an index built by an older reader. Manifests from older binaries have no field, read as 0 and rebuild once.
- **Scan cache: only the extractor revision moves.** #575 split the scan cache into a wire version (10, which released clients still read) and `extractor_version`. This PR moves only the extractor revision, `historyScanCacheVersion` 11 → 13. `historyScanCacheWireVersion` stays 10.
  - Revision 12 mines compact tool output, because a revision-11 cache holds scans with no code facts.
  - Revision 13 covers the null/empty `message` fallback below. Earlier builds of this branch wrote revision 12 without that fallback, and their caches would otherwise stay current. I confirmed this with a run: a brain built by one of those builds kept 0 exchanges after a refresh at revision 12, and gets 2 at 13 (`TestHistoryRefreshRescansRevision12NullMessageCache`, with a real fixture).
  - `TestHistoryScanCacheWireCompatibilityAndExtractionInvalidation` follows the constant now.
  - `TestHistoryScanCachePreviousExtractorRevisionRescans` checks that a cache from the previous revision is rescanned rather than reused.
  - `docs/memory-storage-compatibility.md` now says revision 13.
- **Short-term overlay: format stays 3 and gains `extractor_version`.** An earlier version of this PR bumped `historyShortTermVersion` 3 → 4 instead. That made every existing v3 overlay load as unsupported on upgrade, so recent sessions held only in the overlay fell back to the long-term index until the next delta. A build without the change also couldn't read a v4 overlay. I confirmed both by running them. Now the overlay keeps format 3 and records the extraction revision. A delta carries an unchanged file's entry forward only when the overlay's `extractor_version` matches the current revision. So an old overlay with an empty entry for a compact transcript is still readable, and that file is re-parsed on the next delta. Removing the reuse check, or not writing the field, each makes `TestHistoryDeltaRescansOverlayFromPreCompactReader` fail. Until that delta runs, the overlay doesn't count as complete coverage. Otherwise `doctor` would say "short-term memory covers the gap" for entries an older extractor built. Instead it reports partial coverage and names `refresh delta`, which `TestShortTermOverlayStatesNeverClaimCoverage` checks.
  - Only earlier builds of this branch ever wrote version 4 (no main commit or release did). Such an overlay has the v3 layout without `extractor_version`, so it's now read as v3 with an unknown extractor: it stays in retrieval, isn't counted as complete, and the next delta rewrites it as v3. Before this, the overlay loaded as unsupported and doctor said to upgrade. `TestHistoryShortTermReadsLegacyV4Overlay` uses a real overlay written by one of those builds. Version 4 is reserved now, so the "unknown newer overlay" health test uses 5.
- **Doctor flags an index from an older extractor.** `history_freshness` used to compare only session fingerprints, so it said "built from the current exported sessions" for an index that `refresh` would rebuild. It now warns and names `refresh` (`TestDoctorHistoryFreshnessFlagsOlderExtractor`). The warning, and the overlay's partial-coverage text, give the revision and say whether it's older or newer than this binary's. Before, data from a newer binary was also called "older". Behaviour is unchanged: any other revision is re-parsed, as with the scan cache.
- **One shared helper.** `transcriptRecordContent` returns a `user`/`assistant` record's content in either shape (nested under `message`, otherwise top-level `content`). It replaces the separate fallbacks #557 added in each reader. Those fallbacks disagreed on an edge case: `"message":{}` or `null`. A null or empty `message` now counts as absent, and `TestTranscriptRecordContentPrecedence` pins the order.

## Commits

1. fix(history): read compact v1 transcripts in history and conversation readers
2. fix: Version persisted history indexes
3. fix(history): invalidate short-term overlays from the pre-compact reader
4. fix(history): treat a null or empty message as absent in transcriptRecordContent
5. fix(history): keep the overlay format at v3 and gate reuse on extractor_version
6. fix(history): don't count an older extractor's overlay as complete coverage
7. fix(history): keep v4 overlays from the pre-release build readable
8. fix(history): move the extraction revision to 13 for the null-message fallback
9. fix(doctor): flag a history index built by an older extractor
10. fix(doctor): name a newer extractor revision as newer, not older

Commit 5 reverses commit 3's version bump while keeping its test, and commits 6–10 follow from review of that. I can squash them if you prefer.

## Tests

The new tests are in `internal/cli/history_compact_transcript_test.go`, with fixtures written by hand from the format spec for claude-code, codex and pi.

Everything below was run at f66dbe8c in a clean `env -i` environment (Linux amd64, go 1.27.3):

- `mise run lint` passes.
- `mise run test:prepush` passes (`go test ./... -count=1`, gofmt, vet).
- `go test -race -count=1` passes on `./internal/cli/`, `./internal/cli/internal/manifest/` and `./internal/cli/patterns/`.

## Upgrade cost: one rescan

Moving the extractor revision to 13 makes every existing brain rescan its transcripts once and rebuild its history index on the next `refresh`. That covers released brains at revision 11 and brains built by earlier builds of this branch at revision 12. It's the same one-time cost as any extractor-revision bump. Overlays from another revision stay readable and are re-parsed by the next `refresh delta`.

## Compatibility notes

- **Released clients.** I built v0.4.0 from its pinned commit. Once a current build writes a brain, its manifest is schema 5 (#590), and v0.4.0's `privacy verify` and `refresh delta` already refuse that brain with `memory_unsupported_version`. So the overlay and scan-cache changes here don't add a new break for released clients.
- **The new `extraction_version` manifest field.** A build from after #590 but before this PR can't rewrite a manifest that has the field, because `LoadForReplace` rejects unknown fields. I confirmed this by running it. Readers ignore the field. Main has added manifest fields the same way without a schema bump, so I left it. #564 adds the same kind of field to the pattern source.

## What was NOT verified

- The unit-test fixtures were written by hand from the spec and the CLI's converter source, not captured from a live `entire` checkpoint.
- Real data, run before the rebase on the earlier head against main f8deab17 and not repeated: real compact checkpoints from entire-brain's own refs (newest 400: 91 Claude Code, 5 Codex, 7 Pi sessions). History records went from 101,957 to 142,657. Only code-fact records changed: Claude Code 20,770 → 59,164, Pi 369 → 2,675. Codex and all other record kinds were unchanged.
- Upgrading a real v0.4.0-built brain was also run before the rebase only.
- `-race` covered only the three packages above. Not run on macOS or Windows.
- Watch alone doesn't rebuild an index from an older extractor when sessions are unchanged. Memory reconciliation goes by session input digests (0 jobs created in a run on the revision-12 fixture), so only `refresh` rebuilds the index. The same is true on main for its 10 → 11 bump. Not changed here; doctor now says to run `refresh`.
- After upgrading, `refresh delta` can treat every transcript as short-term material and fill the capped overlay until a full `refresh` consolidates. This happens on every extractor-revision bump. Not changed here.

## Relation to #564

#564 fixes the other readers (`episode_tools.go`, `recall_evidence_source.go`, `pattern_corpus_enrich.go`). It's based on `main` and doesn't depend on this PR. The link points to Beehtrix's comment on issue #412 (history index stays empty). They opened PR #560 and ask if you want it narrowed or closed.

What I verified:

- **Your #557 (merged Oct 29) fixed the main symptom** — compact `v:1` transcripts reading as 0 records / 0 exchanges. The PR correctly claims only the remainder.
- **Main still lacks the PR's changes.** On current main, `tool_use` blocks ignore the compact dialect's inlined `result.output` (`internal/cli/history.go:2163`), so compact sessions lose tool-output code facts. `historyScanCacheVersion` is still 11, there is no `extraction_version` manifest field, and the `transcriptRecordContent` helper is absent. Their real-data run showed Claude Code code-fact records go from ~20k to ~59k.

- **Related items:** companion PR #564 (other readers) is still open and independent. Issues #412, #534, and #411 are all still open. CI gates on the PR are neutral; only Copilot has commented.

One caveat: the PR bumps the extractor revision to 13, so every existing brain rescans and rebuilds its history index on the next `refresh`. That is the normal one-time cost of a revision bump.

# Review PR

Review a pull request with structured, actionable feedback.

## Arguments

- `` — PR number, URL, or branch name. If empty, review the current branch's open PR.

## Process

### 1. Fetch PR context

```
gh pr view <pr> --json title,body,baseRefName,headRefName,additions,deletions,changedFiles,commits,author
gh pr diff <pr>
```

Read the PR description carefully — it defines scope and intent. Everything you review should be evaluated against what the PR is trying to accomplish.

### 2. Understand the change

Before reviewing line-by-line:
- What is this PR doing and why?
- What files are touched and what's the blast radius?
- Are there any architectural implications?

### 3. Review with this checklist

**Correctness**
- Does the code do what the PR description says?
- Are there logic errors, off-by-one bugs, or unhandled edge cases?
- Are error paths handled correctly?

**Security**
- Any injection risks (SQL, XSS, command injection)?
- Are secrets, tokens, or credentials handled safely?
- Are inputs validated at system boundaries?

**Testing**
- Are there tests for the new/changed behavior?
- Do tests cover edge cases, not just the happy path?
- Are test assertions meaningful (not just "doesn't throw")?

**Design**
- Does the change follow existing codebase patterns and conventions?
- Is the abstraction level appropriate (not over/under-engineered)?
- Are there unnecessary changes outside the stated scope?

**Performance**
- Any N+1 queries, unbounded loops, or missing pagination?
- Are there opportunities for batching or caching that were missed?
- Will this scale with the data sizes it will encounter?

**Readability**
- Are names clear and consistent with the codebase?
- Is complex logic adequately explained?
- Would a future reader understand the "why" behind non-obvious decisions?

### 4. Adversarial review

Take a second, adversarial pass over the diff. Actively try to break the change — assume it has flaws and hunt for them across:

- **Performance** — worst-case inputs, hot paths, allocations, contention.
- **Stability** — race conditions, partial failures, retries, resource leaks, crash recovery.
- **Correctness** — inputs and states that violate the author's assumptions.
- **Simplicity** — code that could be deleted or replaced with something simpler/stdlib.
- **Platform design standards** — deviations from the platform's established design patterns and conventions.

Add any findings to the output using the same severity format.

### 5. Run /simplify

Run the `/simplify` skill (via the Skill tool) against the changed code and fold its findings into the review output.

### 6. Structure your output

For each finding, use this format:

**[severity] file:line — short title**
Description of the issue and why it matters. Include a suggested fix when possible.

Severity levels:
- **[blocking]** — Must fix before merge. Correctness bugs, security issues, data loss risks.
- **[important]** — Should fix. Design problems, missing tests for critical paths, performance issues.
- **[nit]** — Nice to fix. Style, naming, minor improvements. Don't block merge on these.
- **[question]** — Not necessarily wrong, but needs clarification or discussion.

### 7. Summary

End with a brief summary:
- Overall assessment (approve / request changes / needs discussion)
- What the PR does well
- Top 1-3 items that need attention
- Any scope concerns (changes that seem unrelated to the stated goal)

## Guidelines

- Review what's in the diff, not what you wish was there. Don't request unrelated refactoring.
- If the PR is large, focus on the most impactful files first.
- Be specific — "this could be better" is not useful. Show what "better" looks like.
- Distinguish between "this is wrong" and "I would do this differently." Only the former is blocking.
- If you're unsure about something, use [question] severity instead of asserting it's wrong.
- Read relevant source files (not just the diff) when you need context about how changed code integrates with the rest of the system.

435	+// TestHistoryDeltaRescansOverlayFromPreCompactReader pins the upgrade path
436	+// for the short-term overlay. A delta run with the pre-compact reader stored
437	+// compact transcripts as entries with no records, and the delta carries an
438	+// entry forward without re-parsing when the file's size, mtime and content
439	+// digest still match. After upgrading, the old scan cache no longer loads,
440	+// so the transcript is short-term material again; the overlay written by the
441	+// old reader must be rejected and the transcript re-scanned, not carried
442	+// forward empty.
443	+func TestHistoryDeltaRescansOverlayFromPreCompactReader(t *testing.T) {
444	+	brainDir, source := buildConversationBrainFixtureWithTranscript(t, "sess-codex", compactCodexTranscriptFixture)
445	+	const rel = "sessions/main/20260801T120000Z_fix-lock.jsonl"
446	+	cache := loadHistoryScanCache(brainDir)
447	+	entry, ok := cache.Files[rel]
448	+	if !ok || entry.ContentDigest == "" {
449	+		t.Fatalf("fixture scan cache has no content identity for %s: %+v", rel, cache.Files)
450	+	}
451	+	// What the previous binary left on disk: a scan cache from the older
452	+	// extraction version (it no longer loads), and an overlay pinned to the
453	+	// current long-term build whose entry for this transcript is empty.
454	+	cache.Version = historyScanCacheVersion - 1
455	+	saveHistoryScanCache(brainDir, cache)
456	+	if got := loadHistoryScanCache(brainDir); len(got.Files) != 0 {
457	+		t.Fatalf("an older scan cache must not load: %d files", len(got.Files))
458	+	}
459	+	const preCompactOverlayVersion = 3
460	+	stale := shortTermIndex{
461	+		Version:           preCompactOverlayVersion,
462	+		ReconcilerVersion: historyShortTermReconcilerVersion,
463	+		BaseGeneratedAt:   source.GeneratedAt,
464	+		GeneratedAt:       source.GeneratedAt.Add(time.Minute),
465	+		Files: map[string]shortTermFile{
466	+			rel: {Size: entry.Size, ModUnixNano: entry.ModUnixNano, ContentDigest: entry.ContentDigest},
467	+		},
468	+	}
469	+	data, err := json.Marshal(stale)
470	+	if err != nil {
471	+		t.Fatal(err)
472	+	}
473	+	if err := brainstore.WriteBrainRelativeFileAtomic(brainDir, historyShortTermPath, append(data, '\n'), 0o600); err != nil {
474	+		t.Fatal(err)
475	+	}
476	+	// The old overlay's format is still readable: until the next delta its
477	+	// records keep serving retrieval rather than vanishing on upgrade.
478	+	if _, state := loadHistoryShortTermState(brainDir, source); state != shortTermStateCurrent {
479	+		t.Fatalf("pre-upgrade overlay state = %s, want %s (readable)", state, shortTermStateCurrent)
480	+	}
481	+
482	+	stats, err := buildHistoryShortTermLocked(brainDir, source.GeneratedAt.Add(time.Hour))
483	+	if err != nil {
484	+		t.Fatalf("delta: %v", err)
485	+	}
486	+	if stats.Reused != 0 || stats.Scanned != 1 {
487	+		t.Fatalf("delta stats = %d reused / %d scanned, want 0/1: the empty entry from the old reader was carried forward", stats.Reused, stats.Scanned)
488	+	}
489	+	overlay, state := loadHistoryShortTermState(brainDir, source)
490	+	if state != shortTermStateCurrent {
491	+		t.Fatalf("overlay state after delta = %s, want %s", state, shortTermStateCurrent)
492	+	}
493	+	if overlay.Version != preCompactOverlayVersion || overlay.ExtractorVersion != historyScanCacheVersion {
494	+		t.Fatalf("overlay version/extractor = %d/%d, want %d/%d", overlay.Version, overlay.ExtractorVersion, preCompactOverlayVersion, historyScanCacheVersion)
495	+	}
496	+	// An overlay written by the current extractor is reused, not re-parsed.
497	+	stats, err = buildHistoryShortTermLocked(brainDir, source.GeneratedAt.Add(2*time.Hour))
498	+	if err != nil {
499	+		t.Fatalf("second delta: %v", err)
500	+	}
501	+	if stats.Reused != 1 || stats.Scanned != 0 {
502	+		t.Fatalf("second delta stats = %d reused / %d scanned, want 1/0", stats.Reused, stats.Scanned)
503	+	}
504	+	overlay, _ = loadHistoryShortTermState(brainDir, source)
505	+	exchanges := 0
506	+	for _, record := range overlay.Files[rel].Records {
507	+		if record.Kind == conversationKind {
508	+			exchanges++
509	+		}
510	+	}
511	+	if exchanges != 2 {
512	+		t.Fatalf("overlay exchanges for the compact transcript = %d, want 2 (records: %d)", exchanges, len(overlay.Files[rel].Records))
513	+	}
514	+}

@@ -0,0 +1,78 @@
+package cli
+
+import (
+	"encoding/json"
+	"os"
+	"path/filepath"
+	"testing"
+	"time"
+
+	"github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/cli/internal/brainstore"
+)
+
+// testdata/history_short_term_v4.json is an overlay written by a pre-release
+// build of this change (cab0496c) that stamped historyShortTermVersion 4 and
+// had no extractor_version field. Its layout is the v3 layout. A brain that
+// ran that build must keep serving the overlay's records after the upgrade,
+// and the next delta must re-parse them (their extractor is unknown) and
+// rewrite the overlay as v3.
+func TestHistoryShortTermReadsLegacyV4Overlay(t *testing.T) {
+	brainDir, source := buildConversationBrainFixtureWithTranscript(t, "sess-codex", compactCodexTranscriptFixture)
+	const rel = "sessions/main/20260801T120000Z_fix-lock.jsonl"
+	data, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join("testdata", "history_short_term_v4.json"))
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+	var fixture shortTermIndex
+	if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &fixture); err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+	if fixture.Version != 4 || fixture.ExtractorVersion != 0 || len(fixture.Files[rel].Records) == 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("fixture is not a v4 overlay with records for %s: version %d extractor %d", rel, fixture.Version, fixture.ExtractorVersion)
+	}
+	// Same state the v4 build left behind: the transcript is short-term
+	// material (its scan cache entry no longer loads) and its size, mtime and
+	// content digest still match the overlay entry, so only the extractor
+	// gate can force the re-parse.
+	cache := loadHistoryScanCache(brainDir)
+	cache.Version = historyScanCacheVersion - 1
+	saveHistoryScanCache(brainDir, cache)
+	mtime := time.Unix(0, fixture.Files[rel].ModUnixNano)
+	if err := os.Chtimes(filepath.Join(brainDir, filepath.FromSlash(rel)), mtime, mtime); err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+	if err := brainstore.WriteBrainRelativeFileAtomic(brainDir, historyShortTermPath, data, 0o600); err != nil {
+		t.Fatal(err)
+	}
+
+	overlay, state := loadHistoryShortTermState(brainDir, source)
+	if state != shortTermStateCurrent {
+		t.Fatalf("v4 overlay state = %s, want %s (readable)", state, shortTermStateCurrent)
+	}
+	if got, want := len(overlay.Files[rel].Records), len(fixture.Files[rel].Records); got != want {
+		t.Fatalf("v4 overlay records = %d, want %d", got, want)
+	}
+	if overlay.complete() {
+		t.Fatal("a v4 overlay's extractor is unknown; it must not count as complete coverage")
+	}
+	if health := memoryOverlayHealth(brainDir, source); health["state"] != shortTermStateCurrent {
+		t.Fatalf("overlay health = %v, want state %s", health, shortTermStateCurrent)
+	}
+	for _, finding := range detectMemoryMigrations(brainDir, source) {
+		if finding.Path == historyShortTermPath {
+			t.Fatalf("v4 overlay reported as %s: %s", finding.State, finding.Action)
+		}
+	}
+
+	stats, err := buildHistoryShortTermLocked(brainDir, source.GeneratedAt.Add(2*time.Hour))
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("delta: %v", err)
+	}
+	if stats.Reused != 0 || stats.Scanned != 1 {
+		t.Fatalf("delta stats = %d reused / %d scanned, want 0/1", stats.Reused, stats.Scanned)
+	}
+	overlay, state = loadHistoryShortTermState(brainDir, source)
+	if state != shortTermStateCurrent || overlay.Version != historyShortTermVersion || overlay.ExtractorVersion != historyScanCacheVersion {
+		t.Fatalf("after delta: state %s version %d extractor %d, want %s %d %d", state, overlay.Version, overlay.ExtractorVersion, shortTermStateCurrent, historyShortTermVersion, historyScanCacheVersion)
+	}
+}

content.content:
48-An assistant line can carry usage with empty content (`"content":[]` or `"content":null`, for example an aborted or thinking-only call): readers that render transcripts should skip it, and readers that count usage must keep it.
49-
50:Claude Code (`Options.Agent` `claude-code`, and `NewClaudeAdapter`; Cursor and Droid keep legacy counts): streaming fragments of one message ID become one line carrying the whole usage row with the strictly highest `output_tokens` (earlier wins ties) and the model of the first fragment that reports one, skipping Claude Code's `<synthetic>` placeholder; `ts` is the last fragment's. The 5m/1h cache-write split is emitted only when both durations are reported. A message with no usage object on any fragment has no model or usage fields. User entries holding only tool results between fragments of one ID do not split the call: the later fragments become separate lines without usage, and the best row stays on the call's first line (the first with visible content, since a thinking-only message has no line), so a call's usage is counted once. Read per-call usage from the full converted transcript: in a checkpoint slice (`ConvertWithBoundary`), a usage row that arrives after a tool result goes to the call's first line, which can sit before the slice boundary.
51-
52-Codex, `response_item` path (rollouts from Codex versions that do not record items): one assistant line per model call, made of the reasoning, message and tool-call items up to the `token_count` that closes it (real order: call, output, `token_count`; outputs attach to their call by `call_id`). Usage is the difference between consecutive cumulative `info.total_token_usage` snapshots, and `ts` is the closing snapshot's when present, otherwise the last item's. Fresh input is `input - cached` clamped at zero; Codex lines carry no cache-write fields. Repeated snapshots and snapshots missing the input, cached-input or output counter are ignored, `reasoning_tokens` needs both adjacent snapshots to report it, and a decrease in any counter stops usage on later lines. A call with usage but no text or tool calls (for example reasoning-only) emits `content: []`, so consumers may see empty assistant lines; a call with neither usage nor content is omitted. Without usable `total_token_usage` snapshots (flat per-event totals are not read), no `token_count` closes a call, so consecutive assistant items merge into one line until the next user line or tool output; with usable snapshots, a tool output does not end its call. After a counter decrease, total snapshots still close calls but carry no usage, starting with the call the decrease closes. With `StartLine`, the last line before the boundary is part of the slice when its tool output or closing snapshot arrives after it (a one-line head overlap, which can repeat that call's usage); a later output for any earlier call lands only on that call's earlier line.
53-
54-Codex, item path (current rollouts; see Blocks): one line per item, not per call. A call is the items up to the `token_count` that closes it, and its usage is computed exactly as on the `response_item` path: the same snapshot differences, fresh input, cached reads and reasoning, the model from `turn_context`, repeated snapshots ignored, and a counter decrease stopping usage. The usage goes on the call's last assistant line, so the call's earlier lines carry none. A call with usage but no assistant line (reasoning only) gets a usage-only line with `"content":null` and no `id`, whose `ts` is the closing snapshot's; other lines keep their item's `ts`. A user message ends the open call. With `StartLine`, the skipped lines seed the usage baseline, and the last line before the boundary is part of the slice when its call's closing snapshot arrives after it (a one-line head overlap).

Review target: `PR 560 (branch pr-560-review, merged tree at /tmp/pr560-merged) — review the PR's changed code for reuse/simplification; report findings only, do not modify the PR`

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

# Review: PR #560 — fix(history): mine compact tool output, rebuild stale history indexes, share one transcript-content helper

Reviewed against current `main` (15bc2373). Author: Beehtrix (external contributor). 827 additions / 46 deletions, 24 files, all in `internal/cli` plus one docs page.

## What I verified (not just read)

- **The PR is still necessary.** Main's `tool_use` case ignores the compact dialect's inlined `result.output`, main is still at scan-cache revision 11, and the manifest has no `extraction_version` field. #557 fixed only the empty-content symptom.
- **The mining reads the correct field.** The ETF spec (`entireio/cli` `transcript/README.md`) defines `result` as `{"output": string, "status": ...}` — `output` is always a string, which is exactly what `jsonString(jsonMap(block["result"])["output"])` reads. A missing `result` degrades to a no-op for native transcripts.
- **It merges and passes on today's main.** I built the merge locally: the only conflict is `docs/memory-storage-compatibility.md`. On the merged tree, all 8 new tests pass, the full `go test ./internal/cli/...` suite exits 0, and `gofmt -s` and `go vet` are clean.
- **No hidden writers or readers were missed.** Graph confirms `saveHistoryShortTerm` has one caller, the overlay readers all go through the two loaders (both normalize legacy v4), and `historySourceManifest` has one production constructor, which sets `ExtractionVersion`.

## Findings

**[important] rebase required — docs/memory-storage-compatibility.md**
GitHub marks the PR CONFLICTING. The Go files auto-merge; only this docs file conflicts. Ask for a rebase before merge.

**[important] internal/cli/distill_cmd.go:2097 — the PR leaves one diverging copy of the dialect rule it centralizes**
`distillConversationText` keeps `if message, ok := obj["message"]; ok { ... }` — key presence, not emptiness. A record with `"message": null` (the exact shape the revision-13 bump and the `history_brain_rev12_null_message` fixture exist for) now indexes correctly but still distills to `""`. The shared helper is one file away: `distillTextBlocks(transcriptRecordContent(obj))`. Either fold it into this PR or make sure #564 covers it; today neither does.

**[question] internal/cli/history_delta.go:245-263 — is the legacy-v4 overlay shim worth keeping forever?**
The v4 stamp was written only by pre-release builds of this branch; no main commit or release shipped it. The overlay is documented as disposable, and the existing `unsupported` path already rebuilds it on the next delta at the cost of minutes of short-term coverage. The shim instead adds `normalizeLegacyShortTerm`, `readableShortTermVersion`, a permanently reserved version number, a test file, and a fixture. Dropping it would delete roughly 80 lines and one implicit coupling (`memory_admin.go:680` is correct only because `loadHistoryShortTermRaw` normalized upstream). Your call — the code as written is correct and tested — but deletion looks like the better trade.

**[nit] internal/cli/history_delta.go:182-243 — loader prologue duplicated**
`loadHistoryShortTermState` and `loadHistoryShortTermRaw` share a verbatim read/unmarshal/normalize prologue; this PR had to apply the same two edits to each. One shared parse helper would prevent drift.

**[nit] internal/cli/history_delta.go:265 — the revision is stamped twice**
`saveHistoryShortTerm` force-stamps `Version` and `ExtractorVersion`, but its only caller already sets both at construction, and `complete()` depends on the construction-time value. Pick one stamping point. Related: `readableShortTermVersion`'s comment says it serves "the loaders", but only `memoryOverlayHealth` calls it.

**[nit] internal/cli/history_cache_compat_test.go:227 and history_compact_transcript_test.go:520 — tests re-implement existing helpers**
The new scan-cache test hand-rolls gzip+write that `saveHistoryScanCache` already does (and the PR's own overlay test uses it); the export test duplicates ~40 lines of `filelessCheckpointFixtureWithTranscript`. Both would shrink by reusing the helpers.

**[nit] internal/cli/history.go:135 — `historyScanCacheVersion` is now a misnomer**
The constant also stamps the manifest and the overlay. Renaming it (e.g. `historyExtractionRevision`) and keeping the full rule's prose in one place (the const block currently shares it with the manifest field and the helper comment) would stop three copies from drifting. The `transcriptRecordContent` comment also carries git-history prose that can go.

**[nit] internal/cli/history.go:2209 — unbounded `strings.Split` on mined tool output**
`extractToolResultFacts` allocates a slice of every line of a possibly huge `result.output` even though it stops at 8 fragments. Same shape as the pre-existing `function_call_output` path, so consistent — just newly exercised on bigger inputs.

## Summary

**Assessment: approve after a rebase; the nits are optional.** No blocking or correctness issues. The core design is at the right depth: one shared helper for the dialect rule, and extractor-revision gating that fixes the general class of "parser changes are invisible to content-based caches" rather than patching revision 12. Test quality is high — real upgrade fixtures, leak assertions, per-agent coverage, and honest "not verified" notes in the PR body.

Top three items: (1) rebase to clear the docs conflict, (2) decide where the `distillConversationText` divergence gets fixed (here or #564), (3) decide whether to keep or drop the v4 overlay shim. The shim is also the one scope concern: it exists only to protect pre-release dogfood data.

One cost to accept knowingly: revision 13 forces every existing brain to rescan transcripts on its next `refresh` — the normal one-time cost of an extractor bump.

Process notes: Brain and Graph preflights passed (Brain dev build, keyword-only; Graph v0.6.0). A targeted `recall` for prior decisions on this work returned no facts, so history came from the issue threads and PR bodies. The simplify pass ran in report-only mode — I did not push fixes to a contributor's branch; its findings are folded in above. I recorded the review outcome as a Brain memory. If you want, I can post this review on the PR (with the rebase ask) as a comment.

# Memory storage compatibility

## Supported release range

Upgrade coverage includes stable v0.2.0, v0.3.0, v0.4.0, and v0.5.0. Nightly
releases and v0.1.0 are outside this matrix.

`scripts/test-memory-storage-compat.sh` builds actual released code from pinned
commits and executes it against isolated repositories and data directories.
The pre-flat writer suite covers v0.2.0 through v0.4.0. The automatic cleanup
suite also covers v0.5.0, including directories produced by its real migration.

## Storage and migration contract

Memory payloads use one schema 3 `facts/store.json` file. Branch is metadata;
memories are visible across branches. The common repository API and hosted
per-fact wire format remain unchanged.

Normal writes and refreshes fold supported legacy layouts into this store.
Migration reads back the published store and compares complete records with the
expected merged result before cleanup. Schema 1 snapshots and schema 2 markers
remain supported migration inputs.

Local migration is one-way. Released v0.2.0 through v0.4.0 clients cannot read the
migrated directory. Hosted interoperability requires separate local stores.
Files written later by an old local client are imported, with a warning to update
that client. This recovery behavior does not make a shared mixed-version store
supported.

There is no storage rollback command. Recovery to an older version requires a
complete pre-migration backup in an isolated environment. Such a backup does not
include later writes. A post-migration bundle is not a downgrade format.

## Before upgrading and recovering

Stop background work and finish active writes before making a backup. Upgrade
all Brain CLI and watcher processes that share the store before restarting them.
Back up the complete Brain data and the repository's checkpoint refs. Include
any global store in the backup. A memory export alone is not a complete backup.

Normal activity resumes interrupted migration and cleanup. Keep recovery files
and the active store intact. If Brain reports corruption, stop other writers and
preserve the data and backup for support.

See [Upgrade and Recover](https://docs.entire.com/guides/brain/upgrade) for the
customer procedure, verification commands, and support links.

## Automatic cleanup

Brain v0.5.1 adds automatic cleanup. Customers do not need a cleanup command,
script, or confirmation prompt.
Normal memory writes, foreground refreshes, and watcher maintenance remove verified
redundant legacy files. Maintenance includes unchanged watcher passes and existing
global stores. It does not create an unused global store or resume paused services.

Cleanup never imports parked records. Existing v0.5.0 copies must be proved
redundant against the active store. Missing records or unexplained differences
remain available for recovery. Cleanup must not restore a deleted memory or
reverse a retraction.

Unknown fields, unknown files, invalid records, corrupt receipts, unsafe paths,
and unsupported formats prevent removal of the affected data. Valid fact files
can be removed while unrelated files in the same directory remain intact.

Small files use a bounded pass under the existing locks. Large-file verification
runs outside the brain write lock. Removal requires the source checksum and
published store checksum to remain consistent with that verification.
A durable receipt records the source bytes verified before unlink. Recovery
rechecks remaining source bytes and resumes after interruption. A busy writer
causes maintenance to defer its work.

`memories storage status --json` reports cleanup state, pending directories,
retained reasons, and recorded reclaimed bytes. The byte count can underestimate
removal if a process exits before recording progress. It is never a deletion gate.
Status, recall, and other read surfaces remain read-only.

## Claude capture requirement

Use Claude Code **2.1.78 or later** with the generated Entire hooks. Check
`claude --version` before installing or refreshing those hooks. Verify capture
with a new Claude session, a file change, and a commit that creates a checkpoint.
A successful Claude command alone does not verify capture.

See [Claude Code](https://docs.entire.com/agents/claude-code#version-and-capture-verification)

Found and fixed. The failure was Windows-only and not a code bug:

- **Cause:** `TestDoctorHistoryFreshnessFlagsOlderExtractor` depends on the new checked-in brain fixture. Windows runners check out with `core.autocrlf`, and the fixture had no eol pin, so `index.json` gained CRLF line endings. Its bytes then no longer matched the manifest's recorded `index_sha256`, `historystore.LoadIndex` rejected the index, and doctor returned early — so the `history_freshness` check the test looks for was never added. The repo's `.gitattributes` already documents this exact failure class for `benchmarks/agent-brain/**`.
- **Reproduced, then fixed.** I reproduced it on macOS with a `core.autocrlf=true` clone (same failure line as CI), added `-text` pins for `internal/cli/testdata/history_brain_rev12_null_message/**` and `history_short_term_v4.json`, and confirmed the test passes under the same CRLF clone.
- **Pushed** commit 13583255 to the PR branch and approved the new fork CI run. It is running now; I am watching it in the background and will report the result. All other jobs (lint, builds, macOS/Ubuntu tests, the other Windows groups, integration) passed on the previous run, so this was the only gap.
